rv.q: Right now — though there’s plenty in Jesa that’s piquant and poignant — neither is quite sharp enough.

The plot is overstuffed, but director Mei Ann Teo’s committed cast is palpably believable as a family; the actors easily flip between rage and compassion, fighting and forgiving as only sisterhood allows.
Anyone with families they love and fight with will find resonance in this equally funny and emotional play.
Jesa gets better as it goes along, sufficiently so that one can understand what the Ma-Yi staff saw in it.
Jesa is fascinating in its revealing a culture and a world most theatergoers know little about.

The kitchen mishaps, drunken truths and existential crises that subsequently arise seem standard for these family sagas (regardless of culture), but the jesa ritual itself — and the women’s casual variations — lends the story greater interest.
But without a big injection of tension, it just feels like watching sisters bicker.
Jesa both honors tradition and liberates it — charting a bold, bracing, and deeply human path for theater.
Grounded in realism with supernatural touches, and supported by a quartet of appealing performances, Jesa uses emotional and cultural specificity to share a universal story of loss and love.
The four perfectly cast actresses feel lived in with their relationships, with old and new secrets used as weapons against each other that could have felt formulaic is surprisingly fresh.
Yi’s lessons in Korean culture, her vivid characters, and the cast’s chemistry make it an enjoyable production.

cn.t: Yi's debut brings cultural specificity to the familiar family drama, with critics praising its fresh Korean American perspective but divided on execution—some call it a masterpiece, while others find the stakes too low to sustain the tension.

vr.q: Despite only being 90 minutes long, it runs out of steam. The acting begins to feel one-dimensional because there's only so much you can excavate from these characters in such a contained scene.
This play is not quite finished yet, but I mean that as an observation, not a criticism... Go if you're interested in seeing a new voice being born.
